findings.diagnosis: The prompt underestimates contra when the remainder supplies essential qualification, scope, or completion — i.e. when the left fragment, though grammatical, would be misleading or changed in truth/value without the following words (qualifiers, temporal/modal frame, 'respectively'/enumeration alignment, or an object/complement supplied later).
findings.evidence: Observed in 9 cases (en_us_1591, en_us_1427, en_us_608, en_us_1192, en_us_1143, en_us_1593, en_us_877, en_us_802, en_us_1514). In each, the policy kept a cut that left a fragment that looked self-contained syntactically but whose meaning is materially altered by what follows (high measured contra; contra_kill=true). They share continuations that provide key qualifications, scope, or completion (e.g. lists ended by 'respectively', predicates completed by an object/phrase, or material that supplies the main clause's temporal/modal frame).

edit.target: 1) Does what follows the cut overturn, negate, limit, or materially change the truth or claim made so far?
edit.text: 1) Does what follows the cut overturn, negate, limit, materially change, or supply essential qualification/scope/completion for the claim made so far?  - Treat as contra not only explicit negation or contradiction but any continuation that would change what a reader/listener reasonably infers from the left fragment read alone. Examples of such continuations: scope or frame-setting words (temporal/modality), enumerations resolved by 'respectively' or indexing, qualifiers that flip an apparent assertion, or any main-clause object/complement or attachment that completes an apparently finished claim. If the remainder would materially change the truth-value, implication, or pragmatic interpretation of the left fragment when read on its own, set contra high (near 1.0).

findings.diagnosis: The incomplete-predicate / detached-head tests are applied too narrowly: cuts that separate a verb (finite or auxiliary), preposition, or other head from the phrase that completes it often get treated as acceptable when they should be scored very low for cohesion and/or high for contra.
findings.evidence: Seen across many cases where policy cuts split predicates or attachments (en_us_1591, en_us_1593, en_us_608, en_us_1192, en_us_1427, en_us_1143, en_us_1514, en_us_339, en_us_877). In each, the problematic cut detached a predicate or an attachment (verb without its object/complement, preposition without its object, or modifier detached from its head), producing low measured H or high contra even though the left side looked syntactically complete.

edit.text:
Additional explicit checklist (apply at every marker):
- Flag as very poor (reduce cohesion sharply / raise contra) any cut that leaves a finite verb, copula, auxiliary, or preposition without its expected object/complement or attachment (e.g. verb with no object, preposition with no complement, separable particle whose partner is on the right).
- Flag splits inside enumerations where an ordinal, index word, or 'respectively' will resolve which item maps to which antecedent.
- Flag cuts that detach a multiword title/name from its core modifier if translating the halves separately would force a risky attachment decision.

Example (Input / Output illustrating the intended judgment):
Input: We <SEG:?> experience <SEG:?> time <SEG:?> as <SEG:?> a <SEG:?> series <SEG:?> of <SEG:?> events.
Output (illustrative scoring decision): We <SEG:90> experience <SEG:10> time <SEG:100> as <SEG:05> a <SEG:04> series <SEG:03> of <SEG:02> events.
(Reason: cutting after 'experience' or 'time' detaches predicates or their complements and should receive very low cohesion/high-contra scores.)
